properties.title: Baja California becomes a state (1952)
properties.label: Baja California state 1952
properties.description: The Northern Territory of Baja California, governed from Mexico City since its creation, was made the 29th state of the federation by a constitutional reform published on 16 January 1952. Irrigated cotton in the Mexicali Valley and the growth of Tijuana and Mexicali beside the US border had given it the population and revenue to stand alone. Its southern limit was the 28th parallel.
properties.note: Drawn from the modern state of Baja California (Natural Earth). The 1952 limit with the southern territory was the 28th parallel, as it still is; islands are simplified.

sources.citation: Constitución Política de los Estados Unidos Mexicanos, art. 43, as reformed by decrees published in the Diario Oficial de la Federación on 16 Jan 1952 and 8 Oct 1974 (Suprema Corte de Justicia de la Nación, historical texts of art. 43).
Michael C. Meyer, William L. Sherman and Susan M. Deeds, The Course of Mexican History, 10th ed. (Oxford University Press, 2014).

properties.title: The last federal territories become states (1974)
properties.label: New states 1974
properties.description: A constitutional reform published on 8 October 1974, under Luis Echeverría, made the territories of Baja California Sur and Quintana Roo states, leaving the Federal District as the only part of Mexico outside the state system. Both were thinly populated frontiers being opened by federal investment, above all tourism: La Paz and Los Cabos in the south of the peninsula, and Cancún in Quintana Roo.
properties.note: Drawn from the modern states of Baja California Sur and Quintana Roo (Natural Earth). Quintana Roo's boundaries with Yucatán and Campeche were later disputed in the courts; the modern lines are shown.

sources.citation: Constitución Política de los Estados Unidos Mexicanos, art. 43, as reformed by decrees published in the Diario Oficial de la Federación on 16 Jan 1952 and 8 Oct 1974 (Suprema Corte de Justicia de la Nación, historical texts of art. 43).
Michael C. Meyer, William L. Sherman and Susan M. Deeds, The Course of Mexican History, 10th ed. (Oxford University Press, 2014).

properties.title: The Bracero Program begins (1942–1964)
properties.label: Bracero Program
properties.description: With the United States at war and short of farm labour, the two governments agreed in an exchange of notes of 4 August 1942 to send Mexican men to work on US farms under government-supervised contracts. In 1942 recruits were gathered at the Estadio Nacional in Mexico City, where crowds of applicants waited for weeks; later the contracting moved to centres in the Bajío and the north. Renewed after the war and placed on a new legal footing by US Public Law 78 in 1951, the program issued some 4.6 million contracts, to perhaps two million individual men, before Congress let it lapse at the end of 1964.
properties.note: Marked at the site of the Estadio Nacional (1924), demolished around 1949–50 to make way for the Centro Urbano Presidente Juárez housing complex, which was in turn wrecked by the 1985 earthquake.
properties.modern_place: Jardín Ramón López Velarde, Ciudad de México

sources.citation: Bracero History Archive (Roy Rosenzweig Center for History and New Media et al.), "About" (program overview, 1942–1964).
Deborah Cohen, Braceros: Migrant Citizens and Transnational Subjects in the Postwar United States and Mexico (University of North Carolina Press, 2011).
Ernesto Galarza, Merchants of Labor: The Mexican Bracero Story (McNally & Loftin, 1964).
Thomas H. Simmons and R. Laurie Simmons, "Rio Vista Bracero Reception Center", National Historic Landmark nomination (US National Park Service, 2021; designated 2023).
Paul Gillingham, Mexico: A 500-Year History (Atlantic Monthly Press, 2025), ch. 20.

properties.title: Bracero contracting centre at Irapuato
properties.label: Irapuato (braceros)
properties.description: As demand grew, recruitment spread from the capital to the densely populated centre-west, the region that had sent most migrants north since the 1900s. Irapuato, a rail junction in Guanajuato, was one of the five migratory stations named under the 1951 agreement, with Monterrey, Chihuahua, Guadalajara and Aguascalientes.
properties.note: Marked at the city; the station's site is not recorded in the sources used. Recruiting is reported at Irapuato from the mid-1940s, but the sources used document the station only from 1951. Its closing date is uncertain: by 1955 the interior stations had been reduced in favour of the north.

sources.citation: Thomas H. Simmons and R. Laurie Simmons, "Rio Vista Bracero Reception Center", National Historic Landmark nomination (US National Park Service, 2021; designated 2023).
Deborah Cohen, Braceros: Migrant Citizens and Transnational Subjects in the Postwar United States and Mexico (University of North Carolina Press, 2011).

properties.title: Bracero migratory station at Guadalajara
properties.label: Guadalajara (braceros)
properties.description: Guadalajara was one of the five migratory stations set up under the 1951 agreement, in the heart of the old migrant-sending region of Jalisco and Michoacán. US growers wanted stations near the border to cut transport costs, while Mexico wanted them in the interior to discourage men from crossing without papers; by 1955 Guadalajara had been replaced by stations in Sonora.
properties.note: Marked at the city centre; the station's exact site is not recorded in the sources used.

sources.citation: Thomas H. Simmons and R. Laurie Simmons, "Rio Vista Bracero Reception Center", National Historic Landmark nomination (US National Park Service, 2021; designated 2023).
Deborah Cohen, Braceros: Migrant Citizens and Transnational Subjects in the Postwar United States and Mexico (University of North Carolina Press, 2011).

properties.title: Bracero migratory station at Chihuahua
properties.label: Chihuahua (braceros)
properties.description: One of the first five migratory stations of 1951 and one of three still operating at the end of the program. Men selected here went by rail or bus to the Rio Vista reception centre outside El Paso, about 350 km to the north, and from there to farms in Texas, New Mexico, Colorado and the northern plains.
properties.note: Marked at the city centre; the station's exact site is not recorded in the sources used.

sources.citation: Thomas H. Simmons and R. Laurie Simmons, "Rio Vista Bracero Reception Center", National Historic Landmark nomination (US National Park Service, 2021; designated 2023).
Catherine C. Lavoie, "Rio Vista Bracero Reception Center", Historic American Buildings Survey HABS TX-3626 (US National Park Service, 2023).

properties.title: Bracero migratory station at Monterrey
properties.label: Monterrey (braceros)
properties.description: The migratory station closest to the border, about 220 km from Laredo, and one of the three that operated to the end of the program. It fed the Texas reception centres at Eagle Pass and Hidalgo, from which braceros went to cotton fields in Texas and the Arkansas Delta and to farms across the Midwest.
properties.note: Marked at the city centre; the station's exact site is not recorded in the sources used.

sources.citation: Thomas H. Simmons and R. Laurie Simmons, "Rio Vista Bracero Reception Center", National Historic Landmark nomination (US National Park Service, 2021; designated 2023).
Deborah Cohen, Braceros: Migrant Citizens and Transnational Subjects in the Postwar United States and Mexico (University of North Carolina Press, 2011).

properties.title: Bracero contracting centre at Empalme
properties.label: Empalme (braceros)
properties.description: In the mid-1950s the contracting shifted toward the northwest, and the centre at Empalme, the railway town beside Guaymas on the Sonora coast, became one of the program's busiest. Thousands of aspirants from all over Mexico waited there for weeks in the desert heat; in 1960 men selected in the afternoon could be at the El Centro reception centre in California, some 650 km away, by the next morning.
properties.note: The US sources call it the Guaymas station. Córdoba Ramírez and most Mexican accounts date the Empalme centre to 1955–1964; one press account gives 1954.

sources.citation: Thomas H. Simmons and R. Laurie Simmons, "Rio Vista Bracero Reception Center", National Historic Landmark nomination (US National Park Service, 2021; designated 2023).
Diana Irina Córdoba Ramírez, "Vivencias del trabajo agrícola en el Programa Bracero" (interview with the former bracero Guillermo Estrada Moreno), BiCentenario: El ayer y hoy de México no. 49 (2025).
Deborah Cohen, Braceros: Migrant Citizens and Transnational Subjects in the Postwar United States and Mexico (University of North Carolina Press, 2011).

properties.title: El Centro bracero reception centre
properties.label: El Centro reception centre
properties.description: The largest of the US reception centres, in California's Imperial Valley, where braceros were medically examined, fumigated, given identity cards and contracted to growers' associations. It processed more than 1.5 million contracts between 1951 and 1964, many of them for workers from Empalme bound for California's farms.
properties.note: The centre stood near Danenberg Drive and Farnsworth Lane on the south side of El Centro; its buildings were demolished in 2008–09.

sources.citation: Thomas H. Simmons and R. Laurie Simmons, "Rio Vista Bracero Reception Center", National Historic Landmark nomination (US National Park Service, 2021; designated 2023).
Ernesto Galarza, Merchants of Labor: The Mexican Bracero Story (McNally & Loftin, 1964).

properties.title: Nogales bracero reception centre
properties.label: Nogales reception centre
properties.description: Built by the Arizona growers' cooperative and leased to the federal government, this was the smallest of the long-running reception centres, handling about 142,000 contracts, mostly for farms in Arizona and Utah. Its work passed to El Centro when it closed.
properties.note: The building, at Terminal Drive about 4.5 km north of the border, survives in altered form as produce warehouses.

sources.citation: Thomas H. Simmons and R. Laurie Simmons, "Rio Vista Bracero Reception Center", National Historic Landmark nomination (US National Park Service, 2021; designated 2023).

properties.title: Rio Vista bracero reception centre
properties.label: Rio Vista (El Paso)
properties.description: After a few months in the El Paso Coliseum, the El Paso reception centre moved in 1951 to the county poor farm at Socorro, 20 km southeast of the city. Rio Vista processed some 800,000 contracts, sending braceros to Texas, New Mexico, the Rocky Mountain states and the upper Midwest. It is the best-preserved reception centre and was designated a US National Historic Landmark in 2023.

sources.citation: Thomas H. Simmons and R. Laurie Simmons, "Rio Vista Bracero Reception Center", National Historic Landmark nomination (US National Park Service, 2021; designated 2023).
Catherine C. Lavoie, "Rio Vista Bracero Reception Center", Historic American Buildings Survey HABS TX-3626 (US National Park Service, 2023).

properties.title: Eagle Pass bracero reception centre
properties.label: Eagle Pass reception centre
properties.description: Built beside the international bridge to Piedras Negras, Eagle Pass was one of three reception centres that stayed open until the program ended in December 1964, taking over the work of Hidalgo after 1963. It drew on the station at Monterrey and supplied Texas and Midwestern growers.
properties.note: The centre stood directly east of the international bridge; its buildings were torn down in the 1980s and the site is now a US Customs and Border Protection station.

sources.citation: Thomas H. Simmons and R. Laurie Simmons, "Rio Vista Bracero Reception Center", National Historic Landmark nomination (US National Park Service, 2021; designated 2023).

properties.title: Hidalgo bracero reception centre
properties.label: Hidalgo reception centre
properties.description: Hidalgo, in the lower Rio Grande Valley opposite Reynosa, replaced a short-lived centre at Harlingen (1951–53). It executed about 807,000 contracts, peaking in 1955, and sent many braceros to pick cotton in the Arkansas Delta and to farms from Georgia to Minnesota.
properties.note: The centre stood about 300 m from the border, on a site now occupied by a US Customs and Border Protection facility. The NHL nomination gives its closure as 1962 in one passage and 1963 in another.

sources.citation: Thomas H. Simmons and R. Laurie Simmons, "Rio Vista Bracero Reception Center", National Historic Landmark nomination (US National Park Service, 2021; designated 2023).
Catherine C. Lavoie, "Rio Vista Bracero Reception Center", Historic American Buildings Survey HABS TX-3626 (US National Park Service, 2023).

properties.title: The violent election of 1940
properties.label: Election of 1940
properties.description: Cárdenas's chosen successor, General Manuel Ávila Camacho, was officially credited with about 94 per cent of the vote against the conservative general Juan Andreu Almazán, who had broken with the official party. In Mexico City on 7 July police, soldiers and armed squads of the official party and the CTM fought Almazán's supporters for the polling stations, and dozens were killed in the capital. The government's own informants believed that Almazán had carried the major cities and the Catholic highlands; he denounced the fraud but did not rebel, and attended Ávila Camacho's inauguration in December.
properties.note: The fighting took place at polling stations across the capital; the point marks the Zócalo, where the CNDH places the main repression. The CNDH gives no exact toll ("decenas"); Wikipedia gives at least 47 dead nationally. Gillingham (ch. 17) argues that the official party probably lost. He also describes Rubén Figueroa, running for Congress in Guerrero that year, killing five voters at a polling station (ch. 18).
properties.modern_place: Plaza de la Constitución, Ciudad de México

sources.citation: Comisión Nacional de los Derechos Humanos, "Represión y asesinato de partidarios del candidato oposicionista Juan Andreu Almazán en el Zócalo, violación del derecho al voto y a la democracia. 7 de julio de 1940" (efeméride).
Albert L. Michaels, "Las elecciones de 1940", Historia Mexicana 21, no. 1 (1971).
Wikipedia, "1940 Mexican general election" (consulted October 2026).
Paul Gillingham, Mexico: A 500-Year History (Atlantic Monthly Press, 2025), ch. 17.

properties.title: Birth of the Parícutin volcano
properties.label: Parícutin
properties.description: On 20 February 1943 a new volcano opened in Dionisio Pulido's cornfield on the Meseta Purépecha in Michoacán and grew to a cone more than 400 m high. Its lava buried the Purépecha villages of Parícutin and San Juan Parangaricutiro, whose church towers still stand above the flow; the inhabitants were resettled, San Juan's at Nuevo San Juan Parangaricutiro. The eruption lasted until 1952.
properties.note: Marked at the summit cone; the buried church of San Juan lies about 5 km to the north-northeast.

sources.citation: James F. Luhr and Tom Simkin, eds., Parícutin: The Volcano Born in a Mexican Cornfield (Geoscience Press, 1993).
Smithsonian Institution, Global Volcanism Program, "Michoacán-Guanajuato" volcanic field (Parícutin).

properties.title: Wheat breeding in the Yaqui Valley and the Green Revolution
properties.label: Yaqui Valley wheat
properties.description: The Rockefeller Foundation's Mexican Agricultural Program (from 1943) bred new wheat varieties, and from 1945 Norman Borlaug ran a second growing season each year in the irrigated Yaqui Valley near Ciudad Obregón, shuttling seed to the highlands. The high-yielding, rust-resistant wheats made Mexico self-sufficient in wheat by the mid-1950s and were spread worldwide by CIMMYT, founded in 1966. The benefits went mainly to large irrigated farms in the northwest, built up by federal dams and canals.
properties.note: Marked at Ciudad Obregón; the experiment station lay in the valley a few kilometres away. Gillingham (ch. 19) notes that at the end of his term, in 1976, Echeverría redistributed about 100,000 hectares of the Yaqui Valley to ejidos.

sources.citation: Joseph Cotter, Troubled Harvest: Agronomy and Revolution in Mexico, 1880–2002 (Praeger, 2003).
Michael C. Meyer, William L. Sherman and Susan M. Deeds, The Course of Mexican History, 10th ed. (Oxford University Press, 2014).
Paul Gillingham, Mexico: A 500-Year History (Atlantic Monthly Press, 2025), chs. 19–20.

properties.title: Massacre in León
properties.label: León 1946
properties.description: The Unión Cívica Leonesa claimed that its candidate had won the municipal election of 16 December 1945 and that the official party's result was a fraud. On the night of 2 January 1946 soldiers and police fired on its supporters in the main square, killing dozens (officially 36; estimates range from eight, the army's figure, to more than a hundred). The federal Senate then removed Guanajuato's governor, Ernesto Hidalgo, and two weeks later the official party was refounded as the Partido Revolucionario Institucional (PRI).
properties.note: Marked at the main square, now Plaza de los Mártires del 2 de Enero, in front of the municipal palace. Gillingham (ch. 17) gives 27 killed.

sources.citation: Comisión Nacional de los Derechos Humanos, "Matanza de León, Guanajuato, de cientos de ciudadanos que defendían su derecho a la democracia. 2 de enero de 1946" (efeméride).
Héctor Figueroa, "Mártires de León cumplen 70 años", Excélsior, 2 Jan 2016.
Michael C. Meyer, William L. Sherman and Susan M. Deeds, The Course of Mexican History, 10th ed. (Oxford University Press, 2014).
Paul Gillingham, Mexico: A 500-Year History (Atlantic Monthly Press, 2025), ch. 17.

properties.title: Gonzalo N. Santos's cacicazgo in San Luis Potosí
properties.label: Santos cacicazgo
properties.description: Gonzalo N. Santos, a revolutionary veteran from the Huasteca, governed San Luis Potosí from 1943 to 1949 and then controlled its politics through his chosen successors, ruling by patronage and intimidation from his lands in the Huasteca. His power broke only in 1958–59, when a civic movement led by the physician Salvador Nava won the mayoralty of the state capital and the federal government abandoned Santos's governor. He became the textbook example of the regional boss on whom the PRI system relied.
properties.note: Marked at the Plaza de Armas and government palace of San Luis Potosí; Santos's own base was his home region, the Huasteca Potosina, which is not mapped separately.
properties.modern_place: Plaza de Armas, San Luis Potosí

sources.citation: Yolanda Esperanza Camacho Zapata, La construcción del régimen político potosino contemporáneo: Gonzalo N. Santos o el esquema político postrevolucionario en San Luis Potosí, 1943–1949 (PhD thesis, UNAM, 2018).
Gonzalo N. Santos, Memorias (Grijalbo, 1984).
Paul Gillingham and Benjamin T. Smith, eds., Dictablanda: Politics, Work, and Culture in Mexico, 1938–1968 (Duke University Press, 2014).
Paul Gillingham, Mexico: A 500-Year History (Atlantic Monthly Press, 2025), ch. 17.

properties.title: Papaloapan Commission and the Miguel Alemán dam
properties.label: Papaloapan dam
properties.description: After floods in the lower Papaloapan basin in 1944, Miguel Alemán's government created the Papaloapan Commission in 1947 on the model of the Tennessee Valley Authority, to control floods, generate power and open the tropical lowlands of Oaxaca and Veracruz to farming. Its centrepiece, the dam at Temascal on the Tonto River (built from 1949 and in service by the mid-1950s), flooded Mazatec lands and forced the resettlement of more than 20,000 people.
properties.note: Displacement figures vary between sources (about 20,000–22,000 Mazatecs).

sources.citation: Thomas T. Poleman, The Papaloapan Project: Agricultural Development in the Mexican Tropics (Stanford University Press, 1964).
David Barkin and Timothy King, Regional Economic Development: The River Basin Approach in Mexico (Cambridge University Press, 1970).
Paul Gillingham, Mexico: A 500-Year History (Atlantic Monthly Press, 2025), ch. 17.

properties.title: Tepalcatepec Commission
properties.label: Tepalcatepec Commission
properties.description: Also in 1947 the government set up a commission for the hot Tepalcatepec basin of Michoacán (the Tierra Caliente), headed by the former president Lázaro Cárdenas. It built dams, canals and roads that turned the valley around Apatzingán into irrigated cotton and fruit country. In 1960 it was enlarged into the Balsas Commission, covering the whole Balsas basin, where the El Infiernillo dam was built and the steel port later named Lázaro Cárdenas was planned.
properties.note: Marked at Apatzingán, the main town of the irrigated district.

sources.citation: David Barkin and Timothy King, Regional Economic Development: The River Basin Approach in Mexico (Cambridge University Press, 1970).
Michael C. Meyer, William L. Sherman and Susan M. Deeds, The Course of Mexican History, 10th ed. (Oxford University Press, 2014).
Paul Gillingham, Mexico: A 500-Year History (Atlantic Monthly Press, 2025), ch. 18.

properties.title: Acapulco becomes a resort
properties.label: Resort Acapulco
properties.description: Linked to the capital by road since the late 1920s, Acapulco was turned into Mexico's first great beach resort in the 1940s and 1950s, above all under Miguel Alemán, who as interior minister and then president promoted the expropriation of beachfront land for hotels and the coastal road named after him. Hollywood stars and foreign investors followed, and the population swelled with migrants who settled in the hills behind the bay to work in the hotels. The resort stood beside one of the poorest and most violent states, a contrast that the dirty war of the 1970s made stark; from the 1970s federal investment shifted to Cancún.
properties.note: Marked on the Costera Miguel Alemán, the hotel strip around the bay. The dates are approximate: Alemán took office in December 1946, and Cancún was begun in 1970. Gillingham (ch. 20) mentions 5,000 squatters settling a single property, the Barranca de la Laja, in early 1958.

sources.citation: BBC News Mundo, "Acapulco: los años dorados y la decadencia de la 'Perla del Pacífico' mexicano", 5 Nov 2023 (republished by 24horas.cl).
Paul Gillingham, Mexico: A 500-Year History (Atlantic Monthly Press, 2025), chs. 17, 18 and 20.

properties.title: Ciudad Universitaria
properties.label: Ciudad Universitaria
properties.description: The National University's new campus was built from 1949 on the lava field of the Pedregal de San Ángel, then at the southern edge of Mexico City, and dedicated on 20 November 1952; most schools moved there in 1954. Planned by Mario Pani and Enrique del Moral with murals by Rivera, Siqueiros and O'Gorman, it is a monument of the "Mexican miracle" and a UNESCO World Heritage Site (2007). Its Olympic Stadium opened the 1968 Games.
properties.modern_place: Torre de Rectoría, Ciudad Universitaria, Coyoacán

sources.citation: UNESCO World Heritage Centre, "Central University City Campus of the Universidad Nacional Autónoma de México (UNAM)", World Heritage List no. 1250 (inscribed 2007).
Michael C. Meyer, William L. Sherman and Susan M. Deeds, The Course of Mexican History, 10th ed. (Oxford University Press, 2014).
Paul Gillingham, Mexico: A 500-Year History (Atlantic Monthly Press, 2025), ch. 18.

properties.title: Repression of the Henriquistas in the Alameda
properties.label: Alameda 1952
properties.description: General Miguel Henríquez Guzmán, a Cardenista who left the PRI to run for the Federación de Partidos del Pueblo Mexicano, was officially given just over 15 per cent of the vote against Adolfo Ruiz Cortines in the election of 6 July 1952. When his supporters gathered in the Alameda Central the next evening for a "victory celebration", police, granaderos and soldiers broke up the crowd with gunfire and tear gas, the shooting went on for hours in the city centre, and more than 500 people were detained. The number of dead was never established. The party was dissolved in 1954, and the centre left stayed inside the PRI for the next three decades.
properties.note: Marked at the Alameda Central. The CNDH cites estimates of the dead from a few dozen up to 500 and the FPPM's list of 524 detainees and 77 to 100 wounded; Gillingham (ch. 17) gives some 500 arrests and 130 wounded collected by ambulances and says that reports of the dead varied greatly.

sources.citation: Comisión Nacional de los Derechos Humanos, "Represión de la 'Fiesta de la Victoria', matanza contra henriquistas en la Alameda; defendían el derecho a la democracia del pueblo de México. 7 de julio de 1952" (efeméride).
Paul Gillingham, Mexico: A 500-Year History (Atlantic Monthly Press, 2025), chs. 17 and 19.

properties.title: Railway workers' movement crushed
properties.label: Railway strike 1959
properties.description: In 1958 railway workers led by Demetrio Vallejo won a wage rise through stoppages and took over their union from its government-backed leaders. When they struck again in early 1959, the government of Adolfo López Mateos declared the strike illegal, the army occupied the railways and, from 28 March, hundreds of workers were jailed and more than 9,000 dismissed. Vallejo spent more than eleven years in Lecumberri prison; the defeat ended the most serious challenge to the official labour system of the period.
properties.note: The movement was national, strongest in the rail centres of Mexico City, Monterrey, San Luis Potosí and Veracruz; the point marks the Buenavista station district of Mexico City, the main terminal.

sources.citation: Comisión Nacional de los Derechos Humanos, efeméride of 28 February (the railway strike of 1959).
Robert F. Alegre, Railroad Radicals in Cold War Mexico: Gender, Class, and Memory (University of Nebraska Press, 2013).
Michael C. Meyer, William L. Sherman and Susan M. Deeds, The Course of Mexican History, 10th ed. (Oxford University Press, 2014).
Paul Gillingham, Mexico: A 500-Year History (Atlantic Monthly Press, 2025), ch. 17.

properties.title: Massacre in Chilpancingo
properties.label: Chilpancingo 1960
properties.description: A broad movement of students, teachers and townspeople demanded the removal of Guerrero's governor, General Raúl Caballero Aburto. On 30 December 1960 soldiers fired on protesters at the Alameda of the state capital, killing 18 or 19 people (some accounts say at least 15). In January 1961 the Senate declared the state's powers dissolved and removed the governor, but the repression convinced activists such as the schoolteacher Genaro Vázquez that peaceful opposition was futile.
properties.note: Marked at the city centre; the shooting was at the Alameda Granados Maldonado by the municipal palace. Sources differ on the day in January 1961 of the Senate's decision (5 or 30 January). Gillingham (ch. 18) gives 21 killed.

sources.citation: Comisión Nacional de los Derechos Humanos, efeméride of 30 December (massacre in Chilpancingo, 1960).
Comisión Nacional de los Derechos Humanos, efeméride of 31 December (the fall of Governor Caballero Aburto, 1961).
Alexander Aviña, Specters of Revolution: Peasant Guerrillas in the Cold War Mexican Countryside (Oxford University Press, 2014).
Paul Gillingham, Mexico: A 500-Year History (Atlantic Monthly Press, 2025), ch. 18.

properties.title: Murder of Rubén Jaramillo and his family
properties.label: Jaramillo 1962
properties.description: Rubén Jaramillo, a former Zapatista who led sugar-cane workers and landless peasants in Morelos, had more than once taken up arms and had been amnestied by López Mateos. On 23 May 1962 soldiers and police took him, his pregnant wife Epifania Zúñiga and her three sons from their house in Tlaquiltenango and shot them near the ruins of Xochicalco. The killing showed how little room the regime left for independent agrarian movements in the land of Zapata.
properties.note: The bodies were found near the Xochicalco archaeological zone; the exact spot is not recorded in the sources used. Jaramillo first led the cane growers and workers of the cooperative Emiliano Zapata mill at Zacatepec in 1942–43 (compare e10-zacatepec-1938) before taking up arms. Gillingham (ch. 17) describes the mill, run by administrators sent from Mexico City, as controlling some 19,000 peasants on 32 ejidos.

sources.citation: Comisión Nacional de los Derechos Humanos, efeméride of 23 May (murder of Rubén Jaramillo and his family, 1962).

Michael C. Meyer, William L. Sherman and Susan M. Deeds, The Course of Mexican History, 10th ed. (Oxford University Press, 2014).
Paul Gillingham, Mexico: A 500-Year History (Atlantic Monthly Press, 2025), ch. 17.

properties.title: Chamizal settlement
properties.label: Chamizal
properties.description: When the Rio Grande shifted south in the 19th century it left El Chamizal, land Mexico had held, on the El Paso side. An arbitration of 1911 largely favoured Mexico but the US refused to accept it. The convention of 29 August 1963 settled the dispute: a new concrete channel was dug, Mexico received the 366-acre Chamizal tract and 264 acres east of Córdova Island and ceded the northern 193 acres of Córdova Island, a net gain of about 437 acres (177 ha); the land was formally transferred on 28 October 1967 at a meeting of presidents Johnson and Díaz Ordaz.
properties.note: Marked at the Parque Público Federal El Chamizal in Ciudad Juárez, on the returned land. The tract is not drawn as a polygon; the convention text and later summaries give different figures for the Córdova Island exchange.

sources.citation: Convention between the United States of America and the United Mexican States for the Solution of the Problem of the Chamizal, signed 29 Aug 1963 (text: International Boundary and Water Commission).
US National Park Service, Chamizal National Memorial, "The Chamizal Convention".

properties.title: Ciudad Nezahualcóyotl
properties.label: Nezahualcóyotl
properties.description: Mexico City grew from about 1.8 million people in 1940 to more than 8 million by 1970, much of the growth in irregular settlements on its edges. On the dry bed of Lake Texcoco, lots sold without services by private developers filled within a few years, and in 1963 the State of Mexico made the settlements a municipality, Nezahualcóyotl. By 1980 it had more than a million inhabitants, one of the country's largest cities.
properties.note: Population figures are approximate and depend on how the metropolitan area is defined.

sources.citation: Diane E. Davis, Urban Leviathan: Mexico City in the Twentieth Century (Temple University Press, 1994).
Michael C. Meyer, William L. Sherman and Susan M. Deeds, The Course of Mexican History, 10th ed. (Oxford University Press, 2014).

properties.title: Border Industrialization Program: Ciudad Juárez
properties.label: Maquiladoras: Juárez
properties.description: With the Bracero Program ended and unemployment high along the border, Mexico launched the Border Industrialization Program in 1965, letting foreign-owned assembly plants (maquiladoras) import parts and machinery duty-free as long as they exported the product. Ciudad Juárez, where the former PEMEX director Antonio J. Bermúdez had run the federal National Border Program (PRONAF) from 1961, became its largest centre, with industrial parks of US electronics, garment and auto-parts plants employing mostly young women.
properties.note: Marked at the city centre. The program dates from 1965; its legal framework was formalised in 1966 and later decrees.

sources.citation: Leslie Sklair, Assembling for Development: The Maquila Industry in Mexico and the United States (Unwin Hyman, 1989).
Kathryn Kopinak, Desert Capitalism: Maquiladoras in North America's Western Industrial Corridor (University of Arizona Press, 1996).
Paul Gillingham, Mexico: A 500-Year History (Atlantic Monthly Press, 2025), chs. 19–20.

properties.title: Maquiladoras: Tijuana
properties.label: Maquiladoras: Tijuana
properties.description: Tijuana, across from San Diego, became the second great maquiladora centre, specialising from the 1980s in electronics; by the 1990s Asian television makers had made it one of the world's largest producers of TV sets. The plants drew migrants from all over Mexico and helped make Tijuana one of the country's fastest-growing cities.
properties.note: Marked at the city centre; the industrial parks are spread around the city, notably at Otay Mesa near the border.

sources.citation: Kathryn Kopinak, Desert Capitalism: Maquiladoras in North America's Western Industrial Corridor (University of Arizona Press, 1996).
Leslie Sklair, Assembling for Development: The Maquila Industry in Mexico and the United States (Unwin Hyman, 1989).

properties.title: Maquiladoras: Nogales, Sonora
properties.label: Maquiladoras: Nogales
properties.description: Nogales, at the Arizona crossing on the Pacific rail and road corridor, was among the first towns to host assembly plants under the 1965 program, and became a centre of electronics and medical-equipment assembly within the "western industrial corridor" running from Tijuana to Juárez.
properties.note: Marked at the city centre.

sources.citation: Kathryn Kopinak, Desert Capitalism: Maquiladoras in North America's Western Industrial Corridor (University of Arizona Press, 1996).
Leslie Sklair, Assembling for Development: The Maquila Industry in Mexico and the United States (Unwin Hyman, 1989).

properties.title: Maquiladoras: Matamoros
properties.label: Maquiladoras: Matamoros
properties.description: Matamoros, across from Brownsville at the mouth of the Rio Grande, was an early maquiladora centre and unusual in that its plant workers were organised from the start by a strong local union, whose contracts gave higher wages and shorter hours than elsewhere on the border.
properties.note: Marked at the city centre.

sources.citation: Leslie Sklair, Assembling for Development: The Maquila Industry in Mexico and the United States (Unwin Hyman, 1989).

properties.title: Maquiladoras: Reynosa
properties.label: Maquiladoras: Reynosa
properties.description: Reynosa, opposite McAllen and already a PEMEX gas and refining centre, grew rapidly as a maquiladora city from the 1970s, part of a lower Rio Grande cluster that with Matamoros and Nuevo Laredo tied Tamaulipas's border economy to Texas.
properties.note: Marked at the city centre.

sources.citation: Leslie Sklair, Assembling for Development: The Maquila Industry in Mexico and the United States (Unwin Hyman, 1989).

properties.title: Attack on the Madera army barracks
properties.label: Madera 1965
properties.description: In the Sierra Tarahumara of Chihuahua, where peasants were fighting timber companies and ranchers for land, a small guerrilla group led by the schoolteacher Arturo Gámiz and the doctor Pablo Gómez attacked the army barracks at Ciudad Madera at dawn on 23 September 1965. The attack, inspired by the Cuban assault on the Moncada barracks, failed: eight guerrillas, including both leaders, were killed, and several soldiers (usually given as five) died. It is usually counted as the start of Mexico's rural and urban guerrilla movements, and the Liga Comunista 23 de Septiembre later took its name from the date.
properties.note: Marked at the town; the barracks were in the town itself. Military casualties differ: most accounts give five soldiers killed, while the CNDH speaks of six soldiers wounded. Gillingham (ch. 18) counts thirteen attackers and says the federal government then sent some 7,000 troops from six states into the region.

sources.citation: Laura Castellanos, México armado, 1943–1981 (Era, 2007).

Fiscalía Especial para Movimientos Sociales y Políticos del Pasado (FEMOSPP), Informe histórico a la sociedad mexicana (Procuraduría General de la República, 2006); draft published by the National Security Archive, Electronic Briefing Book No. 180 (26 Feb 2006).
Comisión Nacional de los Derechos Humanos, efeméride of 23 September (assault on the Madera barracks, 1965).
Paul Gillingham, Mexico: A 500-Year History (Atlantic Monthly Press, 2025), ch. 18.

properties.title: Atoyac and Lucio Cabañas's Party of the Poor
properties.label: Atoyac 1967
properties.description: On 18 May 1967 state judicial police fired on a meeting of parents and teachers in the square of Atoyac de Álvarez on the Costa Grande of Guerrero, killing several people. The rural schoolteacher Lucio Cabañas, whom the police had come to arrest, escaped into the coffee-growing Sierra de Atoyac and built the guerrilla Partido de los Pobres, with a few hundred fighters and wide peasant support. In 1974 his group held the senator and gubernatorial candidate Rubén Figueroa from May to September; Cabañas was killed by the army on 2 December 1974 at El Otatal, in the sierra of Técpan de Galeana.
properties.note: Marked at the town square of Atoyac. El Otatal, where Cabañas died, lies in the sierra of Técpan de Galeana municipality and is not mapped separately. Counts of the dead of 18 May 1967 range from five to eleven. Gillingham (ch. 18) gives seven killed.

sources.citation: Alexander Aviña, Specters of Revolution: Peasant Guerrillas in the Cold War Mexican Countryside (Oxford University Press, 2014).

Fiscalía Especial para Movimientos Sociales y Políticos del Pasado (FEMOSPP), Informe histórico a la sociedad mexicana (Procuraduría General de la República, 2006); draft published by the National Security Archive, Electronic Briefing Book No. 180 (26 Feb 2006).
Comisión Nacional de los Derechos Humanos, efeméride of 2 December (death of Lucio Cabañas, 1974).
Paul Gillingham, Mexico: A 500-Year History (Atlantic Monthly Press, 2025), ch. 18.

properties.title: Genaro Vázquez freed from Iguala prison
properties.label: Genaro Vázquez 1968
properties.description: Genaro Vázquez Rojas, a schoolteacher who had led the Asociación Cívica Guerrerense against Governor Caballero Aburto, was arrested in Mexico City in November 1966 and jailed at Iguala over the deadly clashes there after the state election of December 1962. On 22 April 1968 an armed commando freed him from the prison, and he took his movement, now the Asociación Cívica Nacional Revolucionaria, into guerrilla war in the mountains of Guerrero, kidnapping wealthy men for ransom. He died on 2 February 1972 in Morelia after a road accident; his family alleges he was killed, and the circumstances are disputed.
properties.note: Marked at Iguala. The ACNR operated mainly in the Costa Chica and the sierra; it is not mapped as a zone. Gillingham (ch. 18) calls it Guerrero's state penitentiary; the CNDH and most accounts name the prison at Iguala.

sources.citation: Comisión Nacional de los Derechos Humanos, efeméride of 2 February (death of Genaro Vázquez Rojas, 1972).

properties.title: Massacre of copra producers in Acapulco
properties.label: Acapulco 1967
properties.description: Coconut-copra growers of the Guerrero coast were divided over control of their regional union, run by caciques tied to the PRI and to Governor Raymundo Abarca Alarcón. On 20 August 1967 gunmen and judicial police opened fire on dissidents trying to hold a congress at the union's building in Acapulco; officially 35 people died, but estimates range from about 25 to more than 80. Coming three months after Atoyac, it pushed more of the coast's peasants toward the guerrillas, in sight of the tourist resort.
properties.note: The shooting took place near Avenida Ejido and Calle 6 in central Acapulco; the point marks the city centre.

sources.citation: Francisco Ávila Coronel, "Del clientelismo político a la contrainsurgencia. La masacre de copreros en Acapulco, Guerrero, en perspectiva histórica: 1940-1967", Historia Mexicana 73, no. 4 (2024): 1803–1868.
Comisión Nacional de los Derechos Humanos, efeméride of 20 August (massacre of copra producers in Acapulco, 1967).
Alexander Aviña, Specters of Revolution: Peasant Guerrillas in the Cold War Mexican Countryside (Oxford University Press, 2014).
Paul Gillingham, Mexico: A 500-Year History (Atlantic Monthly Press, 2025), ch. 18.

properties.title: The bazooka at San Ildefonso
properties.label: San Ildefonso 1968
properties.description: A street fight between students on 22 July 1968 and the riot police's brutal response set off clashes in the old university quarter north of the Zócalo. In the early hours of 30 July the army blew open the carved 18th-century door of the Colegio de San Ildefonso, then the UNAM's Preparatoria no. 1, with a bazooka and beat and detained the students inside. The rector, Javier Barros Sierra, protested and led a march on 1 August, and the Consejo Nacional de Huelga formed to unite the city's universities in a strike that lasted until December.
properties.note: Gillingham (ch. 18) calls it "the Poli boarding school"; the building housed the UNAM's Escuela Nacional Preparatoria no. 1 (Gaceta UNAM). He gives about one hundred students handed over to the riot police. His account of the march of 13 September, led by the rector, merges the rector's march of 1 August with the Silent March.
properties.modern_place: Antiguo Colegio de San Ildefonso, Ciudad de México

sources.citation: Gaceta UNAM, "1968: bazucazo contra San Ildefonso; el Ejército asalta CU".
Elena Poniatowska, La noche de Tlatelolco: testimonios de historia oral (Era, 1971).
Paul Gillingham, Mexico: A 500-Year History (Atlantic Monthly Press, 2025), ch. 18.

properties.title: Counterinsurgency and disappearances in the Sierra de Atoyac
properties.label: Dirty war, Atoyac
properties.description: To destroy Cabañas's guerrilla the army occupied the Sierra de Atoyac, set up checkpoints, regrouped villages and detained, tortured and disappeared hundreds of peasants, many held at the Atoyac barracks or flown to Campo Militar No. 1 in Mexico City. The FEMOSPP special prosecutor's report (2006) documents this campaign; Atoyac municipality accounts for a large share of Mexico's disappeared of the 1970s. In 2009 the Inter-American Court condemned Mexico for the disappearance of Rosendo Radilla Pacheco, a composer of corridos taken off a bus at an army checkpoint near Atoyac on 25 August 1974.
properties.note: The campaign covered the whole sierra between the Costa Grande and the Sierra Madre del Sur; the point marks Atoyac de Álvarez, site of the army barracks. Radilla was taken off the bus at a checkpoint at Colonia Cuauhtémoc, between Cacalutla and Alcholoa, on the coastal road near Atoyac. Counts of the disappeared vary by source (the FEMOSPP draft and local organisations give several hundred for Atoyac). Gillingham (ch. 18) counts 1,421 documented army arrests in Guerrero during the dirty war and more than 500 people disappeared, most of them civilians.

sources.citation: Fiscalía Especial para Movimientos Sociales y Políticos del Pasado (FEMOSPP), Informe histórico a la sociedad mexicana (Procuraduría General de la República, 2006); draft published by the National Security Archive, Electronic Briefing Book No. 180 (26 Feb 2006).
Corte Interamericana de Derechos Humanos, Caso Radilla Pacheco vs. Estados Unidos Mexicanos, sentencia de 23 de noviembre de 2009 (Serie C No. 209).
Alexander Aviña, Specters of Revolution: Peasant Guerrillas in the Cold War Mexican Countryside (Oxford University Press, 2014).
Paul Gillingham, Mexico: A 500-Year History (Atlantic Monthly Press, 2025), ch. 18.

properties.title: Death flights from Pie de la Cuesta
properties.label: Death flights
properties.description: In the 1970s prisoners taken in the Guerrero counterinsurgency were brought to Military Air Base no. 7 at Pie de la Cuesta, on the beach west of Acapulco, shot, and dropped from military aircraft into the Pacific. A list published in 2024 names 183 people linked to 25 flights in 1972–74, and Gillingham, drawing on the planes' logs found by military prosecutors, counts 54 flights carrying an estimated 350 bodies between 1974 and 1980. General Mario Arturo Acosta Chaparro was charged in 2002 over the killing of peasants in the 1970s, but the charges were dropped in 2006.
properties.note: Marked at Pie de la Cuesta; the air base lies beside the beach and the Coyuca lagoon. The dates combine the two counts (1972–74 for the 2024 list, 1974–80 for Gillingham, ch. 18); the total of victims is unknown.
properties.modern_place: Pie de la Cuesta, Acapulco, Guerrero, Mexico

sources.citation: Expansión Política, "Dan a conocer lista 183 desaparecidos en 'vuelos de la muerte' de los años 70", 8 Aug 2024.
Wikipedia, "Mario Arturo Acosta Chaparro" (consulted October 2026), for the 2002 charges.
Paul Gillingham, Mexico: A 500-Year History (Atlantic Monthly Press, 2025), chs. 18–19.

properties.title: Massacre at Tlatelolco
properties.label: Tlatelolco 1968
properties.description: The student movement of summer 1968 had filled the Zócalo with demands for the release of political prisoners and the disbanding of the riot police; on 18 September the army occupied Ciudad Universitaria. On the evening of 2 October, ten days before the Olympic Games opened, soldiers and the plain-clothes Olimpia Battalion opened fire on a rally in the Plaza de las Tres Culturas at the Nonoalco–Tlatelolco housing estate. The government acknowledged a few dozen deaths; later estimates run from several dozen to more than 300, and the number has never been established.
properties.note: Gillingham (ch. 18) sets out the range: 26 dead reported in the Mexican press, 44 cases documented in the archives and 325 in The Guardian, with about 150 the figure in popular memory. He calls the Olimpia Battalion the "Batallón Olímpica".
properties.modern_place: Plaza de las Tres Culturas, Ciudad de México

sources.citation: Elena Poniatowska, La noche de Tlatelolco: testimonios de historia oral (Era, 1971).
Julio Scherer García and Carlos Monsiváis, Parte de guerra. Tlatelolco 1968 (Aguilar, 1999).

Paul Gillingham, Mexico: A 500-Year History (Atlantic Monthly Press, 2025), ch. 18.

properties.title: Founding of Cancún
properties.label: Cancún
properties.description: Bank of Mexico planners chose a nearly empty barrier island on the Caribbean coast of the territory of Quintana Roo for a resort built from scratch, to earn foreign exchange and develop the southeast. Work began in 1970 under the tourism trust INFRATUR, which became FONATUR in 1974, the year the first hotels opened. Cancún grew into Mexico's largest resort and the core of the "Riviera Maya", turning the Caribbean coast into the fastest-growing region of the country.
properties.note: 20 April 1970 is the date usually celebrated as the founding; the federal decree is of 1971.

sources.citation: Rebecca Maria Torres and Janet D. Momsen, "Gringolandia: The Construction of a New Tourist Space in Mexico", Annals of the Association of American Geographers 95, no. 2 (2005): 314–335.
Michael C. Meyer, William L. Sherman and Susan M. Deeds, The Course of Mexican History, 10th ed. (Oxford University Press, 2014).
Paul Gillingham, Mexico: A 500-Year History (Atlantic Monthly Press, 2025), ch. 20.

properties.title: The Corpus Christi massacre (Halconazo)
properties.label: Halconazo 1971
properties.description: On 10 June 1971, the feast of Corpus Christi, a student march set out from the Polytechnic's Casco de Santo Tomás in support of students in Monterrey. As it turned toward the Calzada México–Tacuba it was attacked by the Halcones, a paramilitary group trained and paid by the Federal District government, while police looked on. Dozens were killed (40 according to the CNDH; some estimates reach 120). President Echeverría denied responsibility; three decades later the special prosecutor's attempt to try him for genocide failed in the courts.
properties.note: The attack began on Avenida de los Maestros near the Escuela Normal Superior and spread through the San Cosme–Tacuba streets; the point marks the Normal metro station. Gillingham (ch. 18) cites a Gobernación figure of 50 students killed.

sources.citation: Comisión Nacional de los Derechos Humanos, efeméride of 10 June (the Corpus Christi massacre, 1971).

properties.title: Murder of Eugenio Garza Sada
properties.label: Garza Sada 1973
properties.description: On the morning of 17 September 1973 a commando of the Liga Comunista 23 de Septiembre, the largest of the urban guerrilla groups founded in Guadalajara that spring, tried to kidnap Eugenio Garza Sada, patriarch of Monterrey's industrial group, at the corner of Villagrán and Luis Quintanar. He, his driver, his bodyguard and two guerrillas were killed. The Liga kidnapped the British honorary consul and a businessman in Guadalajara the next month; the killing was followed by a campaign of arrests, torture and disappearances against the Liga that destroyed it by about 1981.
properties.note: Marked on Calle Villagrán in central Monterrey; the exact corner was not geocoded. The Liga took its name from the attack on Madera (e11-madera-1965). Its founder, Ignacio Salas Obregón, was captured in 1974 and disappeared.

sources.citation: Excélsior, "La esquina de Villagrán y Quintanar: a 50 años del asesinato de Eugenio Garza Sada", Sep 2023.
Expansión Política, "¿Qué fue la Liga Comunista 23 de Septiembre?", 23 Sep 2019.
Laura Castellanos, México armado, 1943–1981 (Era, 2007).
Paul Gillingham, Mexico: A 500-Year History (Atlantic Monthly Press, 2025), ch. 18.

properties.title: Cantarell oil field
properties.label: Cantarell
properties.description: Oil seeping into the Bay of Campeche, reported by the fisherman Rudesindo Cantarell in the early 1970s, led PEMEX to drill the field in 1976 and find a supergiant offshore deposit some 80 km out to sea. With the onshore Reforma fields of Chiapas and Tabasco (1972), it made Mexico a major exporter: production began in 1979, oil-backed borrowing financed the López Portillo boom, and the collapse of oil prices brought the 1982 debt crisis. Cantarell peaked at about 2.1 million barrels a day in 2004 and has declined steeply since.
properties.note: Marked at the field's published coordinates; the complex covers several fields and platforms. No geocoder check is possible offshore.

sources.citation: George W. Grayson, The Politics of Mexican Oil (University of Pittsburgh Press, 1980).
Wikipedia, "Cantarell Field" (consulted October 2026), for the discovery, coordinates and production history.
Paul Gillingham, Mexico: A 500-Year History (Atlantic Monthly Press, 2025), ch. 19.

properties.title: Operation Condor in the Golden Triangle
properties.label: Operación Cóndor
properties.description: By the mid-1970s Mexico supplied most of the heroin sold in the United States, much of it from the "Golden Triangle" where the Sierra Madre Occidental joins Sinaloa, Durango and Chihuahua. With US money and DEA advisers, the army sent thousands of troops, helicopters and herbicide-spraying aircraft (paraquat and 2,4-D) into the sierra around Badiraguato. Peasant villages suffered torture, killings and forced displacement, and the campaign doubled as counterinsurgency. It cut Mexican heroin for a few years, but it also pushed the Sinaloan traffickers, among them Félix Gallardo, Caro Quintero and Fonseca, to move to Guadalajara, where they formed "the Federation".
properties.note: Marked at Badiraguato, home town of several of the traffickers; the campaign covered the highlands of all three states. Dates differ: Cedillo dates Operación Cóndor proper from January 1977 to 1988; Gillingham (ch. 21) dates the campaign from 1975 to 1979, counting the eradication drive that preceded it.

sources.citation: Richard Craig, "Operation Condor: Mexico's Antidrug Campaign Enters a New Era", Journal of Interamerican Studies and World Affairs 22, no. 3 (1980): 345–363.

Benjamin T. Smith, The Dope: The Real History of the Mexican Drug Trade (W. W. Norton, 2021).
Paul Gillingham, Mexico: A 500-Year History (Atlantic Monthly Press, 2025), ch. 21.

properties.title: Ixtoc I blowout
properties.label: Ixtoc I
properties.description: On 3 June 1979 PEMEX's exploratory well Ixtoc I, in the Bay of Campeche about 100 km northwest of Ciudad del Carmen, blew out and caught fire. It spilled an estimated 3 to 3.5 million barrels over nearly ten months before it was capped on 23 March 1980, one of the largest accidental oil spills in history, fouling beaches from Campeche to Texas.
properties.note: Marked at the well's published coordinates. No geocoder check is possible offshore.

sources.citation: US National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration, Office of Response and Restoration, "IXTOC I" incident record (1979).

properties.title: San Juanico gas explosions
properties.label: San Juanico 1984
properties.description: Early on 19 November 1984 a leak at the PEMEX liquefied-petroleum-gas terminal at San Juan Ixhuatepec, in the northern suburbs of Mexico City, set off a chain of explosions that destroyed much of the surrounding working-class neighbourhood. Around 500 people were killed and thousands injured. The disaster showed how fast the metropolis had grown around industrial installations once built on its edge.
properties.note: Death tolls vary between about 500 and 600.

sources.citation: Diane E. Davis, Urban Leviathan: Mexico City in the Twentieth Century (Temple University Press, 1994).
Michael C. Meyer, William L. Sherman and Susan M. Deeds, The Course of Mexican History, 10th ed. (Oxford University Press, 2014).

properties.title: Murder of the DEA agent Enrique Camarena
properties.label: Camarena 1985
properties.description: In 1984 an army raid on El Búfalo, Rafael Caro Quintero's vast marijuana plantation in the Chihuahua desert, destroyed a crop worked by thousands of labourers; the DEA agent Enrique "Kiki" Camarena had helped locate it. On 7 February 1985 he was seized by five gunmen, one of whom claimed to be a police officer, as he left the US consulate in Guadalajara, and tortured to death; his body was found on 5 March. US pressure brought the arrests of Caro Quintero and Ernesto Fonseca in 1985 and of Miguel Ángel Félix Gallardo in 1989, the end of the Guadalajara-based "Federation" and the dissolution of the Dirección Federal de Seguridad, whose agents had protected the traffickers.
properties.note: Marked at the city of Guadalajara; the consulate's 1985 address is not confirmed in the sources used. El Búfalo, near Jiménez in southern Chihuahua, is not mapped separately.

sources.citation: Drug Enforcement Administration Museum, "Enrique S. Camarena" (Wall of Honor).
Expansión Política, "¿Quién fue Kiki Camarena?", 18 Jul 2022.
Benjamin T. Smith, The Dope: The Real History of the Mexican Drug Trade (W. W. Norton, 2021).
Paul Gillingham, Mexico: A 500-Year History (Atlantic Monthly Press, 2025), ch. 21.

properties.title: Epicentre of the 1985 earthquake
properties.label: 1985 epicentre
properties.description: At 7:17 a.m. (often given as 7:19) on 19 September 1985 a magnitude 8.0 earthquake struck on the subduction zone off the coast of Michoacán, near Lázaro Cárdenas, followed by a magnitude 7.5 aftershock the next evening. The coast close to the epicentre suffered relatively little; the catastrophe was nearly 400 km away in Mexico City, where the soft clays of the old lake bed amplified the long, slow shaking.
properties.note: USGS epicentre, offshore (no geocoder check possible). Gillingham (ch. 19) gives 7:18 a.m. and 8.1 on the Richter scale; the USGS moment magnitude is 8.0.

sources.citation: US Geological Survey, Earthquake Hazards Program, event usp0002jwe, "M 8.0 – 1985 Michoacán, Mexico Earthquake".
S. Suzuki and A. S. Kiremidjian, The Mexico Earthquake of September 1985: A Preliminary Report (John A. Blume Earthquake Engineering Center, Stanford University, 1986).

properties.title: The 1985 earthquake in Mexico City
properties.label: 1985 earthquake
properties.description: Hundreds of buildings collapsed in the centre of the capital, mostly mid-rise structures standing on the lake-bed clays in the Centro, Roma, Doctores, Juárez and Tlatelolco districts; the Hotel Regis, which stood here, burned and fell. Official figures put the dead at several thousand (counts of about 4,000 to 6,000 were given); other estimates exceed 10,000. Its slow, overcentralised response, while neighbours dug out survivors themselves, gave rise to new urban movements and weakened the PRI's hold on the capital.
properties.note: Marked at the Plaza de la Solidaridad beside the Alameda, built on the site of the Hotel Regis. The damage zone corresponds roughly to the old bed of Lake Texcoco (compare e1-lake-texcoco in era 1); it is not drawn separately. Gillingham (ch. 19) gives more than 400 buildings destroyed and between 10,000 and 40,000 dead.
properties.modern_place: Plaza de la Solidaridad, Ciudad de México

sources.citation: Elena Poniatowska, Nada, nadie: las voces del temblor (Era, 1988).
Diane E. Davis, Urban Leviathan: Mexico City in the Twentieth Century (Temple University Press, 1994).
S. Suzuki and A. S. Kiremidjian, The Mexico Earthquake of September 1985: A Preliminary Report (John A. Blume Earthquake Engineering Center, Stanford University, 1986).
Paul Gillingham, Mexico: A 500-Year History (Atlantic Monthly Press, 2025), ch. 19.

properties.title: Collapse of the Nuevo León building, Tlatelolco
properties.label: Nuevo León building
properties.description: In the Nonoalco–Tlatelolco housing estate, two of the three sections of the Nuevo León apartment block, on Paseo de la Reforma, struck each other and collapsed, killing an estimated 200 to 300 residents, who had complained of structural faults for years. With the collapse of the Juárez housing complex, the General Hospital and the Juárez Hospital, it became a symbol of negligence and corruption in public construction. A sundial on the site marks the time of the earthquake.
properties.note: The building stood on Paseo de la Reforma within the estate, a few hundred metres from the Plaza de las Tres Culturas; the point is approximate. Death tolls for the building vary widely in the sources.
properties.modern_place: Plaza de las Tres Culturas, Ciudad de México

sources.citation: Elena Poniatowska, Nada, nadie: las voces del temblor (Era, 1988).
Diane E. Davis, Urban Leviathan: Mexico City in the Twentieth Century (Temple University Press, 1994).
Paul Gillingham, Mexico: A 500-Year History (Atlantic Monthly Press, 2025), ch. 19.

properties.title: Garment workers and the 19 de Septiembre union
properties.label: Seamstresses' union
properties.description: In the garment district along San Antonio Abad, sweatshops in collapsed buildings had trapped hundreds of seamstresses, and some owners tried to recover machinery before the bodies. Survivors organised and, in October 1985, won registration of an independent union, the 19 de Septiembre, one of the movements born from the earthquake.
properties.note: Marked on Calzada de San Antonio Abad. Given to the month: accounts differ on the exact day of the union's registration. Gillingham (ch. 19) writes that about 200 illegal workshops were exposed and that some 1,600 garment workers were killed; other accounts give several hundred dead.
properties.modern_place: San Antonio Abad, Cuauhtémoc, Ciudad de México

sources.citation: Elena Poniatowska, Nada, nadie: las voces del temblor (Era, 1988).
Paul Gillingham, Mexico: A 500-Year History (Atlantic Monthly Press, 2025), ch. 19.

properties.title: The disputed Chihuahua election of 1986
properties.label: Chihuahua 1986
properties.description: After the PAN won Ciudad Juárez and the city of Chihuahua in 1983, the PRI's Fernando Baeza was declared governor of Chihuahua on 6 July 1986 by some 169,000 votes over the PAN's Francisco Barrio, in a count widely denounced as fraud. The opposition answered with marches, road blockades, the taking of international bridges and a 41-day hunger strike by the mayor of Chihuahua, Luis H. Álvarez, and left-wing leaders such as Heberto Castillo came to support them. Baeza took office in October, but the protests prefigured the national campaign for clean elections of 1988; Barrio won the governorship in 1992.
properties.note: Marked at the government palace in the state capital; the protests also centred on Ciudad Juárez and its international bridges.
properties.modern_place: Palacio de Gobierno, Chihuahua, Chihuahua, Mexico

sources.citation: Excélsior, "Alternancia interrumpida; la elección de Chihuahua en 1986", 6 Jul 2016.

properties.title: The disputed election of 1988
properties.label: Election 1988
properties.description: Cuauhtémoc Cárdenas, son of the former president, broke with the PRI and ran at the head of a left-wing front. On election night the vote-counting system run from the Interior Ministry "crashed", and when results resumed Carlos Salinas de Gortari was declared the winner with just over 50 per cent. Cárdenas carried the Federal District, the State of Mexico, Michoacán and other states officially; many believe he won nationally. The ballots were later burned. The PRD, founded in 1989, grew out of his campaign.
properties.note: Marked at the Interior Ministry (Secretaría de Gobernación) on Bucareli, which ran the Federal Electoral Commission's count. The official count gave Cárdenas Baja California, the State of Mexico, Michoacán, Morelos and the Federal District. Gillingham (ch. 19) gives the official shares as 50.5 and 33 per cent and says Salinas was awarded all but three states and Mexico City; the official Federal Electoral Commission figures were about 50.4 and 31 per cent.
properties.modern_place: Palacio de Cobián, Ciudad de México

sources.citation: Jorge G. Castañeda, Perpetuating Power: How Mexican Presidents Were Chosen (New Press, 2000).
Julia Preston and Samuel Dillon, Opening Mexico: The Making of a Democracy (Farrar, Straus and Giroux, 2004).

properties.title: First opposition governor: Baja California
properties.label: Baja California 1989
properties.description: On 2 July 1989 Ernesto Ruffo Appel of the PAN won the governorship of Baja California, and the Salinas government recognised it: the first time since the party's founding in 1929 that the PRI had conceded a state. The opposition advanced from the north and the cities, winning Chihuahua (1992), Guanajuato (1995), Jalisco (1995) and Nuevo León (1997), before the PRI lost the presidency in 2000.
properties.note: Marked at Mexicali, the state capital.

sources.citation: Julia Preston and Samuel Dillon, Opening Mexico: The Making of a Democracy (Farrar, Straus and Giroux, 2004).
Michael C. Meyer, William L. Sherman and Susan M. Deeds, The Course of Mexican History, 10th ed. (Oxford University Press, 2014).
Paul Gillingham, Mexico: A 500-Year History (Atlantic Monthly Press, 2025), ch. 19.

properties.title: Guadalajara sewer explosions
properties.label: Guadalajara 1992
properties.description: On 22 April 1992 gasoline that had leaked from a PEMEX pipeline into the sewers exploded under the Analco district of Guadalajara, ripping open some 8 km of streets. More than 200 people died, after residents' complaints about the smell of fuel had been ignored. The governor of Jalisco was forced to step down, and in 1995 the PAN won the state.
properties.note: The explosions ran along Calle Gante and neighbouring streets in the Reforma sector, south-east of the historic centre; the point is on Calle Gante. The official toll is about 210; other estimates are higher.

sources.citation: Julia Preston and Samuel Dillon, Opening Mexico: The Making of a Democracy (Farrar, Straus and Giroux, 2004).

properties.title: Murder of Cardinal Posadas Ocampo
properties.label: Cardinal Posadas 1993
properties.description: On 24 May 1993 Cardinal Juan Jesús Posadas Ocampo, archbishop of Guadalajara, was shot dead with five other people in the car park of Guadalajara airport, where he had gone to meet the papal nuncio. The official version is that gunmen of the Arellano Félix (Tijuana) organisation mistook his car for that of Joaquín "El Chapo" Guzmán of the Sinaloa traffickers; many Mexicans, including the archdiocese, believe the state was involved. The first of the three political murders of 1993–94, it showed how powerful the drug organisations had become.
properties.note: The case remains open. Gillingham (ch. 19) notes that the cardinal had called for the governor of Jalisco to resign after the gas explosions of 1992 (e11-guadalajara-1992).
properties.modern_place: Aeropuerto Internacional Miguel Hidalgo, Tlajomulco de Zúñiga, Jalisco

properties.title: NAFTA comes into force
properties.label: NAFTA
properties.description: The North American Free Trade Agreement among Mexico, the United States and Canada, negotiated by the Salinas government and signed in December 1992, took effect on 1 January 1994. It locked in the opening of an economy that until the 1980s had been protected, spread maquiladora-style export manufacturing into the interior and the Bajío, and exposed maize farmers to US imports. Trade moved overwhelmingly by truck and rail through a few border crossings, above all Nuevo Laredo–Laredo. The same trucks carried contraband: by the late 1990s much of the cocaine entering the United States crossed here hidden in containers.
properties.note: Marked at Nuevo Laredo, the busiest land crossing for US–Mexico trade, as a symbol of the trade corridor; NAFTA itself has no single location.

sources.citation: Gary Clyde Hufbauer and Jeffrey J. Schott, NAFTA Revisited: Achievements and Challenges (Institute for International Economics, 2005).

properties.title: Zapatista uprising: San Cristóbal de las Casas
properties.label: EZLN: San Cristóbal
properties.description: In the first hours of 1 January 1994, as NAFTA took effect, the Zapatista Army of National Liberation (EZLN), mostly Tsotsil, Tseltal, Tojolabal and Ch'ol Maya from the highlands and the Lacandon forest, seized San Cristóbal and several other towns of Chiapas. From the balcony of the municipal palace it read its Declaration of the Lacandon Jungle, demanding land, work, health, education, democracy and justice. The rebels withdrew from the city the next day.
properties.modern_place: San Cristóbal de las Casas, Chiapas

sources.citation: Neil Harvey, The Chiapas Rebellion: The Struggle for Land and Democracy (Duke University Press, 1998).
John Womack Jr., Rebellion in Chiapas: An Historical Reader (New Press, 1999).

properties.title: Zapatista uprising: battle of Ocosingo
properties.label: Ocosingo 1994
properties.description: Zapatista columns took Ocosingo, the gateway to the Lacandon canyons, on 1 January. When the army counter-attacked on 2 January a large group of rebels was trapped in and around the town market, and the fighting there was the bloodiest of the uprising, with dozens of rebels killed, some apparently executed. Fighting across the region lasted until the government declared a ceasefire on 12 January.
properties.note: Marked at the town centre; the market lies a few blocks away. Total deaths in the twelve days are given as about 145 officially; other estimates are higher. Gillingham (ch. 19) puts the Zapatista dead at about two hundred.

sources.citation: Neil Harvey, The Chiapas Rebellion: The Struggle for Land and Democracy (Duke University Press, 1998).
John Womack Jr., Rebellion in Chiapas: An Historical Reader (New Press, 1999).

properties.title: Zapatista uprising: Las Margaritas
properties.label: EZLN: Las Margaritas
properties.description: Zapatistas from the Tojolabal region and the colonist settlements of the Lacandon forest took Las Margaritas on 1 January and captured the former governor of Chiapas, General Absalón Castellanos Domínguez, at his ranch nearby; he was held until February. The municipality, which stretches to the Guatemalan border, became one of the core areas of the EZLN.

sources.citation: Neil Harvey, The Chiapas Rebellion: The Struggle for Land and Democracy (Duke University Press, 1998).
John Womack Jr., Rebellion in Chiapas: An Historical Reader (New Press, 1999).

properties.title: Zapatista uprising: Altamirano
properties.label: EZLN: Altamirano
properties.description: Altamirano, a ranching town between the highlands and the canyons where cattlemen and Tseltal communities had long clashed over land, was the fourth town taken by the EZLN on 1 January. After the uprising, peasants occupied many private ranches in the region, and the ranchers organised armed guards in response.

sources.citation: Neil Harvey, The Chiapas Rebellion: The Struggle for Land and Democracy (Duke University Press, 1998).

properties.title: Assassination of Luis Donaldo Colosio
properties.label: Colosio 1994
properties.description: The PRI's presidential candidate, Luis Donaldo Colosio, was shot at the end of a campaign rally in Lomas Taurinas, a hillside colonia of Tijuana, on 23 March 1994; a young factory worker, Mario Aburto, was convicted. Together with the uprising in Chiapas and the murder of PRI secretary-general José Francisco Ruiz Massieu in September, it made 1994 the year the PRI system visibly cracked. Ernesto Zedillo replaced Colosio and won the August election.

sources.citation: Julia Preston and Samuel Dillon, Opening Mexico: The Making of a Democracy (Farrar, Straus and Giroux, 2004).
Michael C. Meyer, William L. Sherman and Susan M. Deeds, The Course of Mexican History, 10th ed. (Oxford University Press, 2014).
Paul Gillingham, Mexico: A 500-Year History (Atlantic Monthly Press, 2025), ch. 19.

properties.title: Murder of José Francisco Ruiz Massieu
properties.label: Ruiz Massieu 1994
properties.description: On the morning of 28 September 1994 the PRI's secretary-general, José Francisco Ruiz Massieu, was shot outside the Hotel Casa Blanca on Calle Lafragua, off Paseo de la Reforma, as he left a party meeting. The gunman said he had been hired through a PRI deputy, Manuel Muñoz Rocha, who vanished. In February 1995 Raúl Salinas, the former president's brother, was arrested as the mastermind; his conviction in 1999 was overturned in 2005. With the murders of Cardinal Posadas and Colosio, the case destroyed the PRI's reputation as the guarantor of order.
properties.note: Gillingham (ch. 19) calls the case the greatest political scandal in Mexican history and gives Raúl Salinas's 1999 sentence as fifty years; Wikipedia gives 27½ years after appeal, and the conviction was overturned in 2005.
properties.modern_place: Hotel Casa Blanca, Lafragua, Ciudad de México

sources.citation: Wikipedia, "José Francisco Ruiz Massieu" (consulted October 2026).

Paul Gillingham, Mexico: A 500-Year History (Atlantic Monthly Press, 2025), ch. 19.

properties.title: February 1995 offensive against the EZLN
properties.label: Offensive of Feb 1995
properties.description: On 9 February 1995, weeks after the peso crisis, President Zedillo announced arrest warrants against the Zapatista leadership and sent the army into the rebel zone. Troops occupied Guadalupe Tepeyac, site of the EZLN's "Aguascalientes" meeting centre, whose inhabitants fled into the forest. Public protest forced a halt, and Congress passed a law for dialogue in March, but the army kept its new bases throughout the conflict zone.

sources.citation: Neil Harvey, The Chiapas Rebellion: The Struggle for Land and Democracy (Duke University Press, 1998).
John Womack Jr., Rebellion in Chiapas: An Historical Reader (New Press, 1999).
Paul Gillingham, Mexico: A 500-Year History (Atlantic Monthly Press, 2025), ch. 19.

properties.title: Aguas Blancas massacre
properties.label: Aguas Blancas 1995
properties.description: On 28 June 1995 Guerrero state police stopped a truck carrying members of the Organización Campesina de la Sierra del Sur to a protest at the ford of Aguas Blancas, in Coyuca de Benítez, and shot 17 of them dead. Video of the scene, doctored by the state government to make it appear the peasants were armed, was later broadcast unedited. Governor Rubén Figueroa Alcocer, son of the senator kidnapped by Lucio Cabañas, took leave in March 1996, and a Supreme Court inquiry then found that he and his officials bore responsibility; no senior official was convicted. On the first anniversary the Ejército Popular Revolucionario made its first public appearance there.
properties.note: The point is the locality of Aguas Blancas; the police stopped the truck at the ford (vado) on the road nearby. Figures other than the official 17 dead (one university study gives 27) are not used. Gillingham (ch. 19) places the massacre "near Atoyac" and calls it the Atoyac massacre; Aguas Blancas is in the neighbouring municipality of Coyuca de Benítez, and the governor fell in March 1996, nine months after it.
properties.modern_place: Aguas Blancas, Coyuca de Benítez, Guerrero

sources.citation: Comisión Nacional de los Derechos Humanos, Recomendación 104/1995 (Aguas Blancas, Guerrero, 14 Aug 1995).

Alexander Aviña, Specters of Revolution: Peasant Guerrillas in the Cold War Mexican Countryside (Oxford University Press, 2014).
Paul Gillingham, Mexico: A 500-Year History (Atlantic Monthly Press, 2025), ch. 19.

properties.title: San Andrés Accords
properties.label: San Andrés Accords
properties.description: Talks between the EZLN and the government in the Tsotsil town of San Andrés Larráinzar produced, on 16 February 1996, agreements on indigenous rights and culture, recognising autonomy for indigenous communities. The government did not implement them, and the constitutional reform finally passed in 2001 fell far short of them, so the Zapatistas built their own autonomous municipalities instead.

sources.citation: Neil Harvey, The Chiapas Rebellion: The Struggle for Land and Democracy (Duke University Press, 1998).
John Womack Jr., Rebellion in Chiapas: An Historical Reader (New Press, 1999).

properties.title: La Realidad
properties.label: La Realidad
properties.description: After the 1995 offensive the Zapatista command moved deeper into the Lacandon forest, and the Tojolabal settlement of La Realidad, near the Guatemalan border, became its main point of contact with the outside world. Meetings with government negotiators and visitors were held there, and the first "Intercontinental Encounter for Humanity and against Neoliberalism" (27 July–3 August 1996), which drew thousands of people from more than 40 countries, opened at Oventik and closed at La Realidad. It became the seat of a Zapatista caracol in 2003.

sources.citation: Neil Harvey, The Chiapas Rebellion: The Struggle for Land and Democracy (Duke University Press, 1998).
John Womack Jr., Rebellion in Chiapas: An Historical Reader (New Press, 1999).

Subcomandante Marcos (EZLN), "Primer Encuentro Intercontinental por la Humanidad y contra el Neoliberalismo: discurso de clausura y Segunda Declaración de La Realidad" (La Realidad, 3 Aug 1996), Chiapas no. 3 (Instituto de Investigaciones Económicas, UNAM, 1996).

properties.title: Acteal massacre
properties.label: Acteal 1997
properties.description: On 22 December 1997 a paramilitary group linked to local PRI supporters attacked displaced Tsotsil members of the pacifist Catholic group Las Abejas while they prayed in the hamlet of Acteal, in Chenalhó municipality, killing 45 people, most of them women and children. State police nearby did not intervene. The massacre exposed the paramilitary violence in the highlands that followed the failure of the peace talks; in September 2020, in a friendly settlement before the Inter-American Commission covering some of the victims, the federal government acknowledged the state's responsibility.

properties.title: Cárdenas elected to govern Mexico City
properties.label: Mexico City 1997
properties.description: Under the electoral reforms of the 1990s, which in 1996 made the Federal Electoral Institute fully independent of the government, the capital elected its own head of government for the first time on 6 July 1997. Cuauhtémoc Cárdenas of the PRD won by a wide margin, and the same day the PRI lost its majority in the Chamber of Deputies, also for the first time. Three years later it lost the presidency.
properties.note: Marked at the Antiguo Palacio del Ayuntamiento on the Zócalo, seat of the Federal District government. Gillingham (ch. 19) calls the electoral institute by its later name, the INE (since 2014).
properties.modern_place: Antiguo Palacio del Ayuntamiento, Ciudad de México
